title: Euclid’s view of the Perseus cluster of galaxies
caption: The Perseus Cluster of galaxies, imaged by ESA’s Euclid space telescope
celestial: Perseus Cluster · constellation Perseus · about 240 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi

recognition.text: One of Euclid’s first five full-color images (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Look closely and nearly every smudge here is a galaxy. Euclid’s view holds about 1,000 galaxies belonging to the Perseus Cluster, and more than 100,000 others farther in the background, each containing up to hundreds of billions of stars.

Many of those faint background galaxies had never been seen before, and the light from some of them traveled 10 billion years to reach us. The Perseus Cluster itself is “only” about 240 million light-years away. It is one of the most massive structures known, with thousands of galaxies bathed in a vast cloud of hot gas.

Astronomers have shown that clusters like this one could only have formed if dark matter exists. By mapping where galaxies sit and how their shapes are subtly distorted, Euclid will help work out how dark matter shaped the universe. The observations behind this picture took just five hours.
scale: Using the source’s listed field of view (44 × 44 arcminutes) and the source’s distance of about 240 million light-years, the frame spans roughly 3.1 million × 3.1 million light-years. Its light set out about 240 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Euclid combined its visible-light camera (VIS) with near-infrared measurements in the Y and H bands from its NISP instrument. Blue shows light at about 0.7 microns, green about 1.1 microns and red about 1.7 microns.
understand.eye: Two of the three colors are near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and the mapping was chosen for looks: hot stars read white-blue and dusty regions red.

explore: This was the first time a single image captured so many of the cluster’s galaxies in such fine detail. The six spikes on bright stars come from diffraction in Euclid’s optics, and a few faint, fuzzy blue circles are “optical ghosts,” ordinary artifacts of a complex optical system that don’t affect the science.
alt: A field crowded with galaxies of many sizes, with countless tiny red galaxies farther behind and a few bright foreground stars.
